title: Types and Causes of Sports Injuries
description: Acute and chronic sports injuries — their causes, symptoms and whether they affect soft or hard tissue.
content_html:
Acute vs Chronic Injuries

The R180 specification divides sports injuries into two fundamental categories. Acute injuries are caused by a single sudden traumatic event — a collision, a fall, a missed landing. They have an immediate onset, with pain typically felt instantly. Chronic injuries, by contrast, develop gradually through repetitive movement and overuse; the athlete may notice a dull ache that worsens over weeks or months rather than a sharp pain at a defined moment. Distinguishing these two categories is the foundation of Topic Area 3, and the distinction comes up in both short-answer and extended-response exam questions.

Soft Tissue vs Hard Tissue Injuries

Injuries are also classified by which type of body tissue is damaged. Soft-tissue injuries involve muscles, tendons, ligaments, cartilage or skin. Hard-tissue injuries involve bone, including fractures and dislocations. This classification helps to determine treatment: hard-tissue injuries typically require imaging (X-ray) and immobilisation, while soft-tissue injuries may be managed with PRICE therapy and physiotherapy.

Acute Soft-Tissue Injuries: Strains and Sprains

A strain is a tear or overstretching of a muscle or tendon. Strains occur when a muscle is asked to generate force it cannot sustain — for example, a sprinter pulling their hamstring during maximum acceleration, or a weightlifter straining their lower back. Strains are soft-tissue injuries. A sprain, by contrast, is a tear of a ligament — the fibrous tissue that connects bone to bone and stabilises joints. Sprains most commonly affect the ankle, knee and wrist. The most clinically significant ligament in sport is the Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL), located in the knee: ACL injuries typically occur during sudden direction changes, landing from a jump, or deceleration — making them particularly common in football, netball and basketball. Both strains and sprains are acute soft-tissue injuries.

Key Fact

A strain is a torn or overstretched muscle or tendon (soft tissue). A sprain is a torn ligament (soft tissue). The Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) in the knee is the most clinically important ligament in sport science and is commonly injured through sudden twisting or deceleration movements.

Acute Skin Damage: Abrasions, Contusions and Blisters

Skin damage encompasses four types in the specification. Abrasions (grazes) occur when the skin surface is scraped against a hard surface — a rugby player sliding on an artificial pitch or a cyclist falling on a road. Cuts and lacerations involve a break in the skin caused by sharp contact with an implement, a surface or an opponent. Contusions (bruises) result from a direct blow that damages blood vessels beneath the skin without breaking the surface — the bleeding is internal, causing the characteristic discolouration. Blisters are fluid-filled pockets beneath the skin caused by repetitive friction — a rower's hands, a runner's heels and a tennis player's fingers are all common sites. All of these are soft-tissue injuries. They vary in severity: lacerations and contusions can occasionally be serious (a deep laceration may require suturing; a contusion on the head may mask a more serious injury), while abrasions and blisters are typically minor but can become infected if poorly managed.

Acute Hard-Tissue Injuries: Fractures and Dislocations

A fracture is a break in a bone. The specification distinguishes two types. An open (compound) fracture is where the broken bone penetrates through the skin — highly visible, carries a serious infection risk and always requires emergency medical attention. A closed (simple) fracture is where the bone breaks internally without breaking the skin, identified by pain, swelling, deformity and loss of function. A dislocation occurs when the bones of a joint are forced out of their normal anatomical alignment — the shoulder (glenohumeral joint) and fingers are the most commonly dislocated joints in sport. Dislocations are hard-tissue injuries. They typically cause immediate severe pain, a visible deformity and complete loss of normal joint function. Fractures and dislocations must not be manipulated in the field without medical expertise — a suspected fracture or dislocation should be immobilised and the athlete referred immediately to emergency services.

Key Fact

Hard-tissue injuries in R180 are limited to fractures (open and closed), stress fractures and dislocations. Every other named injury in the specification — strains, sprains, abrasions, contusions, blisters, concussion, tendonitis, epicondylitis and shin splints — is a soft-tissue injury.

Concussion is a traumatic brain injury caused by a blow or jolt to the head that temporarily disrupts normal brain function. Symptoms include headache, confusion, dizziness, nausea, memory problems and sensitivity to light. The specification (3.1.8) requires you to know the possible link between repeated head injuries and the onset of dementia and Alzheimer's disease. This link has become a major safeguarding concern in contact sports, particularly rugby union and American football. Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE) — a degenerative brain condition found post-mortem in former contact sport athletes — is now associated with a history of repeated concussive and sub-concussive blows. As a result, national governing bodies (NGBs) have introduced strict return-to-play protocols: no athlete with suspected concussion should return to play in the same session. Concussion is a soft-tissue injury (brain tissue, not bone).

Chronic injuries develop gradually from repetitive overuse. Tendonitis is inflammation of a tendon caused by repetitive stress. The three sites named in the spec are: Achilles tendonitis (posterior heel — common in runners and jumpers); rotator cuff tendonitis (shoulder — common in swimmers, throwers and racket sport players); and patellar tendonitis (knee — common in basketball players and high jumpers, nicknamed "jumper's knee"). Epicondylitis is inflammation of the epicondyle of the humerus (the bony projection at the elbow). Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) causes pain on the outside of the elbow through overuse of the wrist extensor muscles — common in racket sports and repetitive manual tasks. Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) causes pain on the inside of the elbow through overuse of the wrist flexors — common in golf, throwing sports and rock climbing. Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome) cause pain along the inner shin, typically in runners who rapidly increase their training mileage, run on hard surfaces or have poor footwear. Stress fractures are tiny cracks in bone from repetitive loading — unlike other chronic injuries, they are hard-tissue injuries. All tendonitis, epicondylitis and shin splints are soft-tissue injuries.
exam_tip_html: When answering "compare and contrast" questions on acute vs chronic injuries, structure your response around three dimensions: onset (sudden vs gradual), cause (single traumatic event vs repetitive overuse) and typical tissue affected (both can be soft tissue, but only acute injuries include hard-tissue fractures and dislocations as common presentations). For questions on specific injuries, always state whether the injured structure is soft tissue or hard tissue — this earns a mark in questions that ask you to "classify" or "describe" the injury type. Never confuse strain (muscle/tendon) with sprain (ligament).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Acute injuries result from a single sudden traumatic event (fractures, dislocations, strains, sprains, abrasions, contusions, concussion) while chronic injuries develop gradually through repetitive overuse (tendonitis, epicondylitis, shin splints, stress fractures).
  • Hard-tissue injuries are limited to fractures (open and closed), stress fractures and dislocations; all other named injuries in the specification — including strains, sprains, tendonitis and concussion — are soft-tissue injuries.
  • A strain is a torn muscle or tendon; a sprain is a torn ligament — confusing these two is one of the most common errors in R180 exam answers and consistently loses marks.

glossary_terms.definition: An injury caused by a sudden traumatic event during sport, resulting in immediate pain and often requiring urgent treatment — for example, a sprained ankle or a broken bone.
An injury that develops gradually over time as a result of repeated overuse or repetitive stress on a body part, rather than a single traumatic event.
A soft-tissue injury involving a torn or overstretched muscle or tendon, caused by excessive force or a sudden explosive movement.
A joint injury in which the bones of the joint are forced out of their normal position, most commonly affecting the shoulder, fingers and kneecap.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a hard-tissue injury?
A) Contusion
B) Strain
C) Dislocation
D) Tendonitis
State two differences between an acute injury and a chronic injury.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct differences: acute injuries are caused by a single sudden traumatic event / chronic injuries develop gradually over time through repetitive overuse; acute injuries have an immediate onset of pain / chronic injuries have a gradual onset; acute injuries are often linked to a single specific incident / chronic injuries are linked to repeated loading over weeks or months. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a strain and a sprain, giving one example of a sport in which each commonly occurs.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. "a strain involves a muscle and a sprain involves a ligament"). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. "a strain is a tear or overstretching of a muscle or tendon, commonly occurring in sprinters who pull their hamstring during maximum acceleration; a sprain is a tear of a ligament, most commonly affecting the ankle ligaments in a football player who lands awkwardly on an uneven surface"). A further developed explanation that adds the tissue type classification (both are soft-tissue injuries) scores 3 marks. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the causes and symptoms of an ACL (Anterior Cruciate Ligament) injury and give one reason why it is considered a serious sports injury.
practice_questions.marks:
Causes (up to 2 marks): the ACL is typically injured through sudden direction changes (pivoting), landing from a jump with the knee in an uncontrolled position, or deceleration — common in football, netball and basketball; it is a soft-tissue injury involving a tear of the ligament connecting the femur to the tibia (2 marks for causes with mechanism; 1 mark for a basic statement about twisting the knee).
Seriousness (up to 2 marks): an ACL rupture typically requires surgical reconstruction and a 9 to 12 month rehabilitation period, meaning the athlete misses a significant portion of their career; it also increases the long-term risk of knee osteoarthritis (2 marks for a specific developed reason with evidence; 1 mark for a vague statement that it "takes a long time to heal"). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A 16-year-old basketball player has been experiencing a dull ache in the front of her knee for six weeks. It worsens during and after training sessions.

Discuss whether this is more likely to be an acute or a chronic injury and identify two possible injuries from the specification that could explain her symptoms.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion correctly identifying that the gradual onset over six weeks, worsening with repetitive activity (basketball training), is characteristic of a chronic overuse injury rather than an acute traumatic injury. Two plausible named injuries discussed: patellar tendonitis (inflammation of the patellar tendon below the kneecap — common in jumping sports, nicknamed "jumper's knee") and a stress fracture (tiny crack in the patellar or tibial bone from repetitive loading — hard tissue). The distinction between soft-tissue (patellar tendonitis) and hard-tissue (stress fracture) injuries is noted. Both candidates discussed with their causes applied to the scenario.
Secure (3-4 marks): Correctly identifies chronic injury, names two candidates with brief explanation and some reference to basketball.
Developing (2 marks): Identifies chronic vs acute with limited reasoning, or identifies only one injury without discussion.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A national rugby union governing body is developing a new player welfare policy following concerns about the long-term effects of concussion in the sport.

Evaluate the extent to which the risk of concussion and its long-term consequences should influence how rugby union is played and coached at all levels of the game.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation acknowledging that concussion is a serious acute soft-tissue (brain) injury with documented links to dementia and Alzheimer's disease (CTE in post-mortem studies of former players), and that this justifies strict return-to-play protocols, rule changes (e.g. reducing high-tackle height) and better coaching of safe contact technique. The counter-argument considers that rugby is an inherently physical contact sport — excessive restriction changes the fundamental nature of the game; that most recreational players will never develop CTE (the evidence base is drawn largely from high-volume professional players); and that effective coaching of safe technique and robust NGB enforcement of existing rules may manage risk adequately without rule changes that alter the sport's character. A clear substantiated judgement is reached.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two points on each side with some application to the governance scenario and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points largely one-sided or without a clear judgement.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about concussion with little development and no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following correctly describes a strain?
options: A tear or overstretching of a muscle or tendon
A tear of a ligament connecting bone to bone
A break or crack in a bone
Inflammation of a tendon from repetitive overuse

knowledge_checks.q: Lateral epicondylitis — also known as tennis elbow — causes pain on which part of the arm?
A stress fracture is classified as a _____ injury because it involves a tiny crack in a bone caused by repetitive loading over time.
An open fracture differs from a closed fracture because the broken bone _____ in an open fracture, creating a significant risk of infection.
options: displaces but does not break the surface
cannot be seen on an X-ray

knowledge_checks.q: Match each chronic injury to its correct anatomical location.
right: Inside of the elbow — overuse of the wrist flexor muscles
Posterior heel — inflammation of the tendon attaching the calf to the heel bone
Front of the knee — inflammation of the tendon below the kneecap

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between an acute and a chronic sports injury?
flashcard_questions.a: An acute injury results from a single sudden traumatic event with immediate pain, while a chronic injury develops gradually through repetitive overuse over weeks or months.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a strain and which structures does it affect?
flashcard_questions.a: A strain is a tear or overstretching of a muscle or tendon — both are soft-tissue structures — typically caused by a sudden explosive movement or excessive force.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a sprain and which structure does it affect?
flashcard_questions.a: A sprain is a tear of a ligament, the fibrous soft tissue that connects bone to bone and stabilises joints, commonly affecting the ankle, knee and wrist in sport.

flashcard_questions.q: Where is the Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) and how is it commonly injured?
flashcard_questions.a: The ACL is located in the knee, connecting the femur to the tibia; it is commonly injured through sudden direction changes, landing awkwardly or rapid deceleration during sport.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between an open and a closed fracture?
flashcard_questions.a: In an open fracture the broken bone penetrates through the skin; in a closed fracture the bone breaks internally without breaking the skin surface.

flashcard_questions.q: Which injuries in the R180 specification are classified as hard-tissue injuries?
flashcard_questions.a: Only fractures (open and closed), stress fractures and dislocations are hard-tissue injuries; all other named injuries in the specification are soft-tissue injuries.

flashcard_questions.q: What is tendonitis and name the three sites specified in R180?
flashcard_questions.a: Tendonitis is chronic inflammation of a tendon from repetitive overuse; the three sites are the Achilles tendon, the rotator cuff (shoulder) and the patellar tendon (knee).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between tennis elbow and golfer's elbow?
flashcard_questions.a: Tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis) causes pain on the outside of the elbow; golfer's elbow (medial epicondylitis) causes pain on the inside of the elbow through wrist flexor overuse.

flashcard_questions.q: What are shin splints and what typically causes them in runners?
flashcard_questions.a: Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome) cause pain along the inner shin, typically triggered by rapidly increasing training mileage, hard surfaces or inadequate footwear.

flashcard_questions.q: What is concussion and what long-term risk is it linked to in the specification?
flashcard_questions.a: Concussion is a traumatic brain injury caused by a blow to the head; the specification links repeated head injuries to an increased risk of dementia and Alzheimer's disease.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a contusion and how does it differ from a laceration?
flashcard_questions.a: A contusion is a bruise caused by a direct blow that damages blood vessels beneath intact skin, whereas a laceration is a cut that involves a break in.

flashcard_questions.q: How do blisters form during sport and what type of injury are they?
flashcard_questions.a: Blisters are fluid-filled pockets beneath the skin caused by repetitive friction between skin and equipment or clothing; they are classified as a soft-tissue skin-damage injury.
